title: Deep-Learning 'Aging Clocks' Reveal How Organs Age at Different Speeds Across Adulthood
excerpt: A landmark Cell study built a three-tiered system of biological clocks from over a billion data points, finding that the liver ages fastest and that a simple blood test may one day map the aging of every organ.
body:
• Researchers built a 'Digital Aging Twin' framework using data from 2,019 people aged 18 to 91, integrating clinical tests, brain scans, molecular data, and gut microbiome profiles to create biological aging clocks.
  • The study found organs age at strikingly different rates: the liver hits a critical inflection point around age 40, while the brain accelerates at around 50, with two major waves of aging-related change between 40-50 and 60-70.
  • Liver-derived coagulation factors — not just passive markers — were shown to actively drive aging when injected into mice, accelerating decline across the liver, heart, aorta, and kidney.
  • A simplified blood test using 100-108 plasma proteins could one day provide a comprehensive aging assessment for clinical use.

Your liver may be aging faster than your brain — and a blood test might soon tell you exactly how much faster. A major study published in Cell has produced what researchers call the most comprehensive system yet for measuring biological age across individual organs, revealing that the human body does not age uniformly and identifying specific molecules in the blood that actively drive the process.

Building a Billion-Point Dataset

A team from China's Aging Biomarker Consortium, led by researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Zoology and the China National Center for Bioinformation, recruited 2,019 healthy individuals aged 18 to 91 from cities including Beijing, Quzhou, Ningbo, and Nanchang. They collected 240 parameters per person through clinical tests, cognitive and motor function assessments, brain and retinal imaging, gait analysis, and multiple layers of molecular data — DNA methylation, RNA transcripts, proteins, metabolites, and gut microbiome profiles.

The resulting dataset of more than a billion data points formed the foundation for what the team calls the "Digital Aging Twin" — a computational framework designed to quantify aging at the individual level.

Three Tiers of Aging Clocks

The framework operates on three levels. The first is a core capacity clock that integrates all 240 physiological indicators to reflect overall functional decline. The second is a multimodal clock that uses deep learning with attention mechanisms to weigh the most informative molecular data layers, predicting chronological age with a mean absolute error of just 3.87 years — outperforming any single data type alone.

The third tier comprises organ-specific clocks for the brain, liver, lungs, muscles, blood vessels, and skin, each built from clinical markers, plasma proteins, and imaging features.

Organs on Different Timelines

One of the study's most striking findings is that organs age asynchronously. The liver reaches a critical aging inflection point around age 40, while the brain's aging accelerates closer to age 50. The analysis also identified two major nonlinear waves of aging-related change: one between ages 40 and 50, and another between 60 and 70.

"The Digital Aging Twin framework represents a fundamental shift in aging science — from description to prediction and from identifying correlations to pinpointing drivers."

— MedicalXpress

From Markers to Drivers

The research went beyond measurement. By analyzing plasma proteomics, stained liver tissue, and conducting experiments with human cell cultures and mouse models, the team identified liver-derived coagulation factors — particularly F13B, F9, and F10 — as direct drivers of aging rather than passive biomarkers.

When human aortic endothelial cells were exposed to these factors, they showed elevated aging markers, impaired blood vessel formation, and increased inflammation. Injecting F13B into mice accelerated aging across multiple tissues, including the liver, heart, aorta, and kidney, accompanied by immune cell infiltration.

Toward a Simple Blood Test

To make the framework clinically practical, the researchers developed simplified "proxy clocks" using just 100 to 108 plasma proteins. These protein-based proxies closely matched the predictions of the more complex clocks, suggesting that a relatively straightforward blood test could one day provide a comprehensive multi-organ aging assessment.

Lifestyle Factors That Move the Needle

The study also identified modifiable lifestyle factors linked to biological aging rates. Greater fruit intake, consistent sleep routines, and moderate walking were associated with slower aging. Smoking, insufficient sleep, and high meal frequency were linked to accelerated decline.

The research is part of China's X-Age Project, a national initiative to build comprehensive aging clocks for the Chinese population. While the current framework relies on cross-sectional data, it is being expanded with longitudinal follow-up and larger, more diverse cohorts — a step that could eventually make personalized aging assessments as routine as a cholesterol check.
